## TL;DR

Air-quality numbers can be compared only when they share a unit, an averaging time (the window the concentration is averaged over) and a form (the rule for which values count, such as the fourth-highest day of the year). A gas can be written as mass per volume, in micrograms per cubic meter (µg m⁻³), or as a mixing ratio, in parts per billion (ppb). Converting between them needs the temperature and the pressure. A standard has three parts: a level, an averaging time and a form. An index such as the US Air Quality Index (AQI) turns a concentration into a 0-to-500 value and a category, and two indexes can label the same air differently.
:::

## Two ways to write the same gas

A gas in air can be counted in two ways. One counts its mass in a volume of air, in µg m⁻³. The other counts its share of the molecules, as a mixing ratio. A mixing ratio of 1 ppb means one molecule of gas for every billion molecules of air.

The conversion uses the ideal gas law. Take a gas with molar mass $M$ in g mol⁻¹, in air at pressure $p$ in pascals and temperature $T$ in kelvin. Then

$$c\ [\text{µg m}^{-3}] = x\ [\text{ppb}] \times \frac{M\,p}{R\,T} \times \frac{1}{1000}$$

where $x$ is the mixing ratio in ppb, $c$ is the mass per volume, and $R = 8.314462$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the gas constant. The factor $M p / (R T)$ tells you how many micrograms one ppb holds.

For ozone ($\text{O}_3$, molar mass 48.00 g mol⁻¹) at 25 °C and one standard atmosphere (1013.25 hPa), the factor is $48.00 \times 101325 / (8.314462 \times 298.15) / 1000 = 1.962$ µg m⁻³ per ppb. So 70 ppb, which is 0.070 ppm, is about 137 µg m⁻³ at those conditions.

Pressure changes the factor. At 795 hPa and 10 °C, roughly the air at a site near 2,000 m (illustrative pressure), one ppb of ozone holds 1.62 µg m⁻³. Figure 1 lets you set the conditions and watch the factor move.

::: {.sim-card}
#### ppb ↔ µg m⁻³

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ppbIn = Inputs.range([0, 200], {value: 40, step: 0.5, label: "Mixing ratio (ppb)"})
viewof gasPick = Inputs.select(["O₃", "NO₂", "SO₂"], {value: "O₃", label: "Gas"})
viewof tempC = Inputs.range([-10, 40], {value: 25, step: 1, label: "Temperature (°C)"})
viewof pressHpa = Inputs.range([700, 1050], {value: 1013.25, step: 0.25, label: "Pressure (hPa)"})

molarMass = ({"O₃": 48.00, "NO₂": 46.01, "SO₂": 64.07})[gasPick]
// µg m⁻³ per ppb = M [g mol⁻¹] × p [Pa] / (R × T [K]) / 1000
factorPerPpb = molarMass * (pressHpa * 100) / (8.314462 * (tempC + 273.15)) / 1000
massNow = ppbIn * factorPerPpb

readoutBox = (label, value, color) => html`<div class="sim-readout"><div class="sim-readout-label">${label}</div><div class="sim-readout-value" style="color:${color}">${value}</div></div>`

html`<div class="sim-readouts">
  ${readoutBox("Mass per volume", massNow.toFixed(1) + " µg m⁻³", "#38bdf8")}
  ${readoutBox("Factor, per ppb", factorPerPpb.toFixed(3) + " µg m⁻³", "#f59e0b")}
</div>`
```

**Figure 1.** Mass per volume for a mixing ratio from 0 to 200 ppb, from the ideal gas law. The gas sets the molar mass (ozone 48.00, nitrogen dioxide 46.01, sulfur dioxide 64.07 g mol⁻¹). Temperature runs from −10 to 40 °C and pressure from 700 to 1,050 hPa. The formula assumes ideal-gas behavior, a close approximation for trace gases in ordinary air.
:::

## A standard has three parts

A standard is a rule that monitor data must meet. It has three parts. The **level** is the concentration limit. The **averaging time** is the period over which the monitor averages, such as 8 hours or one year. The **form** is the statistic compared with the level, such as the highest value in a year or an average over several years.

The US ozone standard uses all three. It is met when "the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O₃ concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm".[^cfr5019] The level is 0.070 ppm. The averaging time is 8 hours. The form is the fourth-highest daily value in each year, averaged over three years. Three higher days do not change that value.

The fine particulate standards follow the same pattern. Fine particulate matter (PM2.5, see [What PM2.5 is](what-pm2-5-is.qmd) for the size cut) has an annual level and a 24-hour level. The 2024 rule lowered the annual level from 12.0 to 9.0 µg m⁻³ and kept the 24-hour level at 35 µg m⁻³.[^epa2024] Before the rule, the annual form was "an annual average standard, averaged over three years". The 24-hour standard uses a 98th-percentile form, averaged over three years.

## Guidelines and standards differ

A guideline is advice from a health body. A US standard is a level the air in an area must meet, judged at monitors; it is not a limit on any single source. The World Health Organization (WHO) gives an annual PM2.5 guideline of 5 µg m⁻³ and a 24-hour guideline of 15 µg m⁻³. Its 24-hour value uses a 99th-percentile form.[^whoaqg2021]

The US annual standard of 9.0 µg m⁻³ is 1.8 times the WHO annual guideline. The US 24-hour standard of 35 µg m⁻³ is 2.3 times the WHO 24-hour guideline.[^epa2024]^,^[^whoaqg2021] These ratios compare levels only. The US uses a 98th percentile and the WHO a 99th, so the ratio of levels is not a ratio of strictness.

## How an index turns concentration into a color

An index maps a concentration onto a scale and attaches a label. The US AQI runs from 0 to 500. Table 1 gives its categories and colors.

| AQI | Descriptor | Color |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 50 | Good | Green |
| 51 to 100 | Moderate | Yellow |
| 101 to 150 | Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups | Orange |
| 151 to 200 | Unhealthy | Red |
| 201 to 300 | Very Unhealthy | Purple |
| 301 and above | Hazardous | Maroon |

**Table 1.** US AQI categories, from the 2024 rule.[^epa2024]

Table 2 gives the concentration at which each category starts, for PM2.5 (24-hour, in µg m⁻³) and ozone (8-hour, in ppm). The full table covers other pollutants, which this post omits. The 2024 rule revised only the PM2.5 column.[^epa2024]

| AQI category | AQI | PM2.5, 24-hour (µg m⁻³) | O₃, 8-hour (ppm) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Good | 0–50 | 0.0–9.0 | 0.000–0.054 |
| Moderate | 51–100 | 9.1–35.4 | 0.055–0.070 |
| Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups | 101–150 | 35.5–55.4 | 0.071–0.085 |
| Unhealthy | 151–200 | 55.5–125.4 | 0.086–0.105 |
| Very Unhealthy | 201–300 | 125.5–225.4 | 0.106–0.200 |
| Hazardous | 301 and above | 225.5 and above | 0.201 and above (see note) |

**Table 2.** Breakpoints for PM2.5 and ozone, from the rule's Table 2.[^epa2024] The rule notes that 8-hour ozone does not define AQI values above 301; those use 1-hour ozone, which this table omits.

The index is worked out one pollutant at a time. The steps are these:

1. Truncate the concentration (cut the extra decimals without rounding): to one decimal place for PM2.5 and to three for ozone.
2. Find the two rows of Table 2 that contain it.
3. Apply linear interpolation, which reads a value off a straight line drawn between two table rows:

$$I_p = \frac{I_{Hi} - I_{Lo}}{BP_{Hi} - BP_{Lo}}\,(C_p - BP_{Lo}) + I_{Lo}$$

where $C_p$ is the truncated concentration, $BP_{Hi}$ and $BP_{Lo}$ are the breakpoints above and below it, and $I_{Hi}$ and $I_{Lo}$ are their AQI values.

4. Round the result to the nearest integer.

The reported AQI is the largest of the pollutant values. "The reported AQI corresponds to the pollutant with the highest calculated AQI."[^epa2024] A day with a moderate PM2.5 value and a high ozone value is therefore reported as an ozone day.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked checks

The rule prints its equation as an image, so the form above is the standard linear interpolation. These two checks come from Table 2:

- PM2.5 of 12.0 µg m⁻³, the old annual level, gives AQI 56 (Moderate).
- PM2.5 of 40.0 µg m⁻³ gives AQI 112 (Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups).
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
aqiLine = [{x: 0, y: 0}, {x: 9.0, y: 50}, {x: 35.4, y: 100}, {x: 55.4, y: 150}, {x: 125.4, y: 200}, {x: 225.4, y: 300}, {x: 325.4, y: 500}]
aqiBandRows = [
  {name: "Good", y1: 0, y2: 50, x2: 350, fill: "#34d399"},
  {name: "Moderate", y1: 50, y2: 100, x2: 350, fill: "#facc15"},
  {name: "Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups", y1: 100, y2: 150, x2: 350, fill: "#fb923c"},
  {name: "Unhealthy", y1: 150, y2: 200, x2: 350, fill: "#f87171"},
  {name: "Very Unhealthy", y1: 200, y2: 300, x2: 350, fill: "#a78bfa"},
  {name: "Hazardous", y1: 300, y2: 500, x2: 325.4, fill: "#7f1d1d"}
]

Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 380,
  marginLeft: 60,
  marginRight: 20,
  x: {label: "24-hour PM2.5 (µg m⁻³)", domain: [0, 350]},
  y: {label: "US AQI", domain: [0, 500], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rect(aqiBandRows, {x1: 0, x2: "x2", y1: "y1", y2: "y2", fill: "fill", fillOpacity: 0.22}),
    Plot.text(aqiBandRows, {x: d => d.x2 - 2, y: d => (d.y1 + d.y2) / 2, text: "name", textAnchor: "end", fill: "currentColor", fontWeight: "600"}),
    Plot.ruleX([9.0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
    Plot.ruleX([35], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "2 3"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 9.0, y: 470, t: "annual standard 9.0"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", textAnchor: "start", dx: 4, fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 35, y: 425, t: "24-hour standard 35"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", textAnchor: "start", dx: 4, fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.line(aqiLine, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.text([{x: 195, y: 230, t: "US AQI"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", textAnchor: "start", fill: "currentColor", fontWeight: "600"})
  ]
})
```

**Figure 2.** US AQI against 24-hour PM2.5 from 0 to 350 µg m⁻³. The line joins the Table 2 breakpoints. Each shaded stripe is one AQI category, and the five bands from Good to Very Unhealthy run across the full width. Hazardous (AQI 301 to 500) runs to 325.4 µg m⁻³, the concentration at AQI 500. Dashed rule: the annual standard of 9.0 µg m⁻³. Dotted rule: the 24-hour standard of 35 µg m⁻³. Source: Table 2.[^epa2024]

The same air can get a different label from a different index. The European Air Quality Index (EAQI) says it "reflects the potential impact of air quality on health, driven by the pollutant for which concentrations are poorest", and it "is defined hourly".[^eaqi] Its PM2.5 bands are concentrations, not a 0-to-500 scale.

At 40 µg m⁻³ both indexes put the air in their third of six bands. Only the words differ: the US index says "Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups" and the EAQI says "Moderate". The bands can also differ. At 55.0 µg m⁻³ the US index gives AQI 149, "Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups" (its third band). The EAQI gives "Poor" (51 to 90 µg m⁻³, its fourth band). The EAQI page does not state the averaging time of its PM2.5 bands, so the comparison is rough.

Figure 3 applies the US index, the WHO ratio and the EAQI band to one value.

::: {.sim-card}
#### What does this number mean?

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pm24 = Inputs.range([0, 300], {value: 40, step: 0.1, label: "PM2.5, 24-hour mean (µg m⁻³)"})

aqiBandsPM = [
  [0.0, 9.0, 0, 50, "Good"],
  [9.1, 35.4, 51, 100, "Moderate"],
  [35.5, 55.4, 101, 150, "Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups"],
  [55.5, 125.4, 151, 200, "Unhealthy"],
  [125.5, 225.4, 201, 300, "Very Unhealthy"],
  [225.5, 325.4, 301, 500, "Hazardous"]
]

// Truncate to 0.1 µg m⁻³, interpolate between the Table 2 breakpoints, round half up.
usAqi = c => {
  const t = Math.floor(c * 10 + 1e-9) / 10;
  const [lo, hi, il, ih, name] = aqiBandsPM.find(([l, h]) => t >= l - 1e-9 && t <= h + 1e-9);
  return {v: Math.round((ih - il) / (hi - lo) * (t - lo) + il + 1e-9), name};
}

// EAQI PM2.5 band upper limits, µg m⁻³. Each integer edge is read as "up to and including",
// so 15.1 to 15.9 falls in Moderate.
eaqiName = c => c <= 5 ? "Good" : c <= 15 ? "Fair" : c <= 50 ? "Moderate" : c <= 90 ? "Poor" : c <= 140 ? "Very poor" : "Extremely poor"

aqiNow = usAqi(pm24)

html`<div class="sim-readouts">
  ${readoutBox("US AQI", aqiNow.v + " · " + aqiNow.name, "#38bdf8")}
  ${readoutBox("WHO 24-hour guideline ratio (value ÷ 15)", (pm24 / 15).toFixed(1) + " ×", "#f59e0b")}
  ${readoutBox("EAQI band", eaqiName(pm24), "#a78bfa")}
</div>`
```

**Figure 3.** Readouts for one 24-hour PM2.5 value from 0 to 300 µg m⁻³. The US AQI truncates the value to 0.1 µg m⁻³, interpolates between Table 2 breakpoints and rounds half up. The WHO ratio divides by the 24-hour guideline of 15 µg m⁻³.[^whoaqg2021] The EAQI band reads each integer edge as an upper limit, so 15.1 to 15.9 µg m⁻³ falls in Moderate. The EAQI is defined hourly; here its band is read for the value you set.
:::

## What this means for you

Check three things before you use an air-quality number to plan outdoor work or compare two places. First, the unit: µg m⁻³ and ppb are not interchangeable, and the conversion depends on temperature and pressure. Second, the averaging time: a 24-hour PM2.5 value and an annual one answer different questions. Third, the index that gave the category, since indexes differ.

A daily value can also hide a bad hour. The 2024 rule recommends, but does not require, that an area also report a sub-daily AQI.[^epa2024] If the hour matters for a decision, look for hourly data. Phone apps often show a short-term reading, such as the latest hour, rather than the 24-hour average this post uses, so check which one your app shows. Employer or state rules set any stop-work threshold, so check those rather than a number from this post. [Why ozone peaks in the afternoon](why-ozone-peaks-in-the-afternoon.qmd) explains why ozone often peaks then.

## Key takeaways

- At 25 °C and 1 atm, 1 ppb of ozone is 1.96 µg m⁻³. The factor falls with pressure, so the same ppb holds fewer micrograms at altitude.
- A standard is a level, an averaging time and a form. The same level with a different form is a different rule.
- The AQI interpolates linearly between breakpoints and reports the pollutant with the highest sub-index. A different index can label the same concentration differently.

## References

[^cfr5019]: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. National primary and secondary ambient air quality standards for ozone. 40 CFR § 50.19 (80 FR 65452, 26 October 2015). https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/part-50/section-50.19
